meta.title: Franklin Martinez, applied AI engineer
meta.description: Franklin Martinez builds LLM systems and measures them before trusting them: justask, docmatch and dgii-ts, with live figures and the numbers behind them.

hero.title: I build LLM systems, and I measure them before I trust them.
hero.abstract: For three and a half years I've built business software with TypeScript, React and .NET, and since February 2026 I work as a Full-Stack AI Engineer. On my own time I build LLM systems that get judged by benchmarks instead of demos. The figures on this page run: one replays real responses from a live demo, one is a library running in your browser, and one plots a benchmark you can trace back to its commit.
hero.note_open: Open to remote roles in applied AI and AI product engineering.
hero.note_figures: Figures 1 to 4 are interactive. Every number links its source.

justask.lead: Turns what a person types into an app's own state: a search result, a table filter, a filled record card. Code finds the candidates, a model picks one label per question with a probability for every label, and a field it isn't sure of stays empty for the person to fill (Fig. 1).
justask.note_demo: The live demo runs in English and Spanish, rate limited and capped at $1 of model spend a day.
justask.note_eval: Each eval set is frozen by checksum, with its pass lines written, before the first model call. Round 4 of the search eval: 24 of 24 picks exact, none invented, 6 of 6 ambiguous requests held, p95 380 ms.
justask.note_eval_link: The eval log, failed rounds included

docmatch.lead: Invoice reconciliation for accounts payable. A vision model reads the invoice, deterministic code checks what it read and matches it against the purchase order and the receiving record, and anything that doesn't add up goes to a person (Fig. 2). Every stage has its number in a benchmark table that names the commit behind it (Fig. 3).
docmatch.status: In progress: extraction, matching, entity resolution and the review pipeline are done.
docmatch.note_ci: A CI gate compares field and line-item F1 for every backend against the merge base and fails a pull request that lowers either.
docmatch.note_data: The benchmark documents can't be redistributed, so Fig. 2 uses the synthetic invoices from the CI corpus.

dgii.lead: A TypeScript library for the DGII, the Dominican tax authority. It validates RNC, cédula, NCF and e-NCF numbers offline, and looks up taxpayers by scraping DGII's web pages with retries and a circuit breaker, because DGII has no public API and shut down its SOAP service in January 2025. Fig. 4 is the library itself, running in this page.
dgii.note_skill: It ships an agent skill, so coding agents learn the library with one command:

domiprop.lead: Rental management for Dominican landlords: expense tracking, the monthly 606 purchase report, lease contracts under Ley 85-25, and reminders before tax deadlines. Built with Next.js, NestJS, Prisma and PostgreSQL. Pre-launch.
domiprop.caption: Fig. 5. The DomiProp dashboard.

brook.lead: A mobile app in development (Expo, TypeScript) that turns the links people save from TikTok, Instagram and the web into a searchable library. Each link is sorted by type, such as a recipe, a place or a product, into typed fields with a confidence badge. Before building the app, I'm running a two-week demand test: a landing page and waitlist on one Cloudflare Worker, with the kill lines written before launch.

fig1.label: Fig. 1
fig1.caption: Three requests sent to justask's live demo on October 11, 2026, replayed with their real responses. Bars show the model's probability for each pick. A field whose pick falls below its gate stays empty.
fig1.empty_why: No vendor is named. Best vendor guess: {name} at {p}.

fig2.label: Fig. 2
fig2.caption: A synthetic invoice from docmatch's CI corpus, with its labeled fields drawn where they sit on the page, then the gate's two rules. The gate needs no model and no label. A reading that fails is kept and never retried, because retrying would shop for a passing answer.
fig2.totals_detail: Not checkable: the invoice shows no amount due, and an unreadable or absent value never fails a rule
fig2.verdict: Verdict: passed, one rule checked and none failed
fig2.next: Next: resolve each line to the catalog, then match the invoice against its purchase order and receiving record.

fig3.label: Fig. 3
fig3.caption: Field F1 against cost per document, on a fixed subset of 100 pinned documents. Up and to the left is better. Each row links the commit that produced it.

fig4.label: Fig. 4
fig4.caption: dgii-ts 0.3.0 from npm, imported by this page. The steps show the check-digit arithmetic; the verdict is the library's own. The example numbers are invented.
fig4.input: An RNC, cédula, NCF or e-NCF
fig4.waiting: Type a number, or pick an example.
fig4.rnc_rule: RNC: digits 1 to 8 times weights 7, 9, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. The remainder of the sum over 11 gives the check digit.
fig4.cedula_rule: Cédula: Luhn. Digits 1 to 10 alternate weights 1 and 2, products over 9 lose 9, and the check digit tops the sum up to a multiple of 10.
fig4.ncf_rule: NCF and e-NCF carry no check digit: the library checks the series letter, the type code and the length.
fig4.whitelist: The library accepts this number from its list of known numbers that break the algorithm.

method.title: Method
method.rules: When a model makes a decision in something I build, I write down how it will be judged before the first call: a frozen eval set, pass lines, a gate that is measured rather than guessed. Failed rounds stay in the record.
method.brief_title: From a brief to a shipped product.
method.brief: Research and a plan go in, and a working product with a QA guide comes out: the data model, the API, and an interface that people without a technical background can use.
method.tooling: Every repo carries written rules and edit hooks, so each change typechecks, lints and validates its schema before it lands. Deep models plan, fast models execute, and the same rules hold both.

exp1.title: Full-Stack AI Engineer
exp1.desc: I own products end to end, from the data model to the frontend. I build a commercial financial-management platform we sell to clients, including multi-currency budgeting with approval workflows, and I take on the harder integrations, such as payment providers. I also lead how the team adopts AI coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor CLI and Codex, and I mentor our interns and junior developers.

exp2.title: Software Developer
exp2.desc: I helped build a shared design system used across the company's products, tuned the data layers so the interface felt faster, and mentored junior developers.

about.title: About
about.caption: Fig. 6. Franklin Martinez.
about.p1: I grew up taking things apart to see how they worked, and I build software the same way: I start with the problem and the people who actually have it, and let that decide the rest.
about.p2: Most of what I build deals with messy real-world rules, like taxes, compliance and internal operations, where getting the small details right matters more than the stack.
about.outside: I run {link}, a YouTube channel that tells the world's oldest stories: myths, monsters and legendary history. The production pipeline behind it is mine too, in Python and Remotion: every claim in a script links its source, every name the narrator says has a checked pronunciation, and each episode stops before it spends past its budget on paid models.
